Mr. Speaker, in a way this is an historic occasion because the Bill 1 have presented to the House of Commons enacts Canada's first lemon law. A lemon law is an enactment that defines a lemon as a motor vehicle that, through continuous defects and malfunction, is useless for the purpose for which it was intended.
The object of the law is to provide the purchaser with a remedy, namely, the right to return to the motor vehicle for a refund of the purchase price.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, March 11, consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-99, an Act to provide borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to resume my remarks which were so rudely interrupted by the five o'clock whistle a couple of days ago. We are talking about Bill C-99, introduced by the Government to request borrowing authority for some $22.6 billion so that it can carry on what it calls its "program".
I want to be very clear about our opposition to the Government's program because 1 do not believe that that program at all serves the interests of the country. We see that very clearly in the kind of Budget which was presented two weeks ago. It is a Budget which completely fails to deal with the staggering problem of unemployment. British Columbia has the highest percentage of long-term unemployed people anywhere in Canada. Victoria, British Columbia, which is represented by two Conservative Members of Parliament-one of whom is in the House-has the highest unemployment of any major metropolitan centre in Canada. This Budget completely fails to address that situation and I outlined some of those concerns when I last spoke.
In addition, the Budget loads unfair tax burdens on ordinary Canadians. That means it is taking money, not only out of their pockets but out of their communities, which will have a further depressing effect upon local economies.
When I previously spoke I referred to our goals for official development assistance. I pointed out that the Government had now reneged a third time on its goal for an Official Development Assistance Program. We will not now reach the goal of 0.7 per cent of our GNP for official development assistance until the twenty-first century. On February 28, after this was announced, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) called a meeting of the ambassadors of different nations to Canada and attempted to explain. He tried to put the situation into perspective by saying:
-our deficit in four or five days was comparable to the total yearly GNP of Lesotho. In a month, it was about equal to the combined GNPs of Liberia. Mauritania, and South Yemen. And in a year, using figures from the lastcst World Development Report, it amounted to the combined total GNPs of Chad. Ethiopia, Mali, Zaire, Malawi, Burkina Fasso, Burundi, Tanzania, Rwanda. Benin, Guinea, Togo and Sierra Leone.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs was attempting to justify Canada's cut-backs in its goals for ODA by saying that our deficit was as great as the yearly GNPs of all these nations combined. Somehow he seemed to feel that that justified these cut-backs. I would like to say that it is quite to the contrary.
The fact that these nations have such small GNPs should underline for all Canadians the desperate needs which they have for development assistance. For us to cut back in the face of that type of need is nothing short of criminal. It underlines the reason why our aid is needed and why we have to move as quickly as possible to the stated goal of 0.7 per cent of our GNP right away instead of postponing it to the 21st century. We do not want to see a repetition of the famine in vast parts of Africa which we saw in 1983, 1984 and 1985.
There were warnings with respect to that famine. Action could have been taken in time to have averted a great deal of the tragedy. But countries such as Canada were too slow to move. We have to move more quickly. By cutting back in our goal for ODA we are removing the capability of our development agency to move and prevent future crises such as this. These cuts prohibit further action. It seems we will have to wait until there is some future crisis. We will then step in and wonder why we did not take action earlier.
I wish to stress that development assistance is not a frill but a necessity to world security. The cut-backs which we have seen in our goals will ultimately perform a disservice, not only to the needy people of the world but to Canadians, since our security depends upon a world which is free from the hunger, want and underdevelopment which characterizes so much of it today.
I wish to say a few words about programs for Indian people because the Government is completely failing to meet their needs. Just a few days ago an article in The Globe and Mail pointed out that the Yukon Indian Development Corporation had been denied its application for funding under the Native Economic Development Program after 18 months of foot-dragging by the Government. It was clear that the reason they were denied the funding was a letter written by the Hon. Member
March 13, 1986

for Yukon, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), who wrote to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) asking that the project be shelved. He said: "This matter should receive no further consideration at this time."
When we look at the Estimates for the coming year we see that there will be a cut of some $25 million to the Economic Development Fund in 1986-87. The Conservatives are as good as anyone else at deploring the terrible conditions which exist on Indian reserves. Yesterday the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development acknowledged that conditions on Indian reserves are deplorable. Yet the Government brings in Estimates which cut by some $25 million the Economic Development Fund, the very thing which Indian communities need in order to get out of the welfare dependency trap.
The Nielsen task force report deals with native programs. It is a report which breathes a very mean spirit. It is completely ignorant of the real situation facing Indians, the Inuit and the Metis people of Canada. It is a report which was obviously written from a Bay Street perspective. It breathes a bottomline mentality. It shows no awareness of the needs of Indian people. It talks about user pay for standards. It talks about minimal standards for small bands, in terms of housing and community infrastructure. It admits that in having these minimal standards less than minimal standards for health will result. What type of situation have we when this type of report can even be tabled in the House of Commons in the year 1986? How can we even begin to consider recommendations which talk about less than minimal standards for health for our native people? We are talking about the year 1986 and not the year 1786.
Just last week I heard tragic news concerning four young teen-agers who were burnt to death in a fire in the Kitimat Indian village. I have particular feelings with respect to this matter since I spent four years living in that village. I married the parents of some of those young people.
The fact is that what happened in Kitimat is not unique to Kitimat but is endemic among Indian villages all over Canada. The federal Fires Commissioner said last week that Indian homes are time bombs just waiting to explode. He said that every year, on average, some 12 Indian people lose their lives in Indian communities as a result of fire. Yet, we have a report tabled by the Deputy Prime Minister which talks about minimal standards for Indian housing and minimal standards for community infrastructure. How can we consider that when we see this type of tragic loss of life?
The Hon. Member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. McCuish) when he was in opposition two or three years ago conducted a study of some of the needs of Indian communities in terms of fire protection. I remember him taking his study and passing pictures around showing some of the deplorable conditions in Indian communities and in Indian homes. The photos depicted some of the fire traps in which Indian people have to live. 1 urge Members opposite to consult their colleague and ask him to dig out this file in order to show them some of these pictures of Indian homes which are nothing more than fire traps. I would then ask them to go to the
Borrowing Authority Act
Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and say: "We will not stand for these types of conditions on Indian reserves. We want to see things better".
I see that my time has expired, Mr. Speaker.

There are a number of other nations which are doing much better than is Canada in this regard. However, we are not that bad.

It is not just a Conservative promise to the people of Canada which the Government is breaking, but a commitment of Canada's people made through our representatives, including the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This is a commitment he made to the needy people of our world. We are going back on that commitment.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East referred to the situation of women and children throughout the world. We can look to the fact that in Africa, for example, some 90 per cent of the agricultural work is done by women. Yet we are cutting back on the support that is being given to Africa. We are cutting back on programs that could help provide safe, potable

water that will reduce disease. We are cutting back on health facilities and I am very concerned about that.
I am pleased to see that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is in the House this morning. I would like to answer the second question put by my colleague about my concern with the Government's policy with respect to Indian people. While on the one hand the Government talks about self-government, on the other it has made cut-backs to such things as economic development. There has been foot dragging and then a denial of the grant to the Yukon Native Indian Development Corporation, a corporation that was trying to get some money so it could help move its people out of this downward spiral of dependency upon welfare and grants and help them get some economic development.
I mentioned the fact that there has been a $25.5 million cut from economic development funds in the Estimates for 1986. We are not seeing anything happening there. Perhaps the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development might want to comment on some of these things.
We have now seen the very mean-spirited task force report on native programs that talks about minimal standards. I do not understand how such an outrageous report could even be tabled in the House.

There should be a process by which the Minister would meet with Indian people to develop a proper formula that will address the needs of the Indian people, rather than the so-called needs of those with a bottom line mentality.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have this opportunity to say a few words with respect to Bill C-99, an Act to provide for borrowing authority. This Act provides that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), with the approval of the Governor in Council, may raise money under the Financial Administration Act by way of a loan to the extent of $22,600 million. That is an awful lot of money but, unfortunately, it is in line with the Government's requirements which came about as a result of the situation that was created through years and years of mismanagement and misspending.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, we have already approved in principle the Budget of February 26. This Bill is the first of a series of Bills necessary to implement the provisions of the Budget that has already been passed in principle. The principles that were set out in the 1986 Budget are the same principles as those followed in the economic statement made by the Minister of Finance in November 1984, and the Budget that the Minister of Finance brought down in May 1985. The Budget of 1986 and the borrowing Bill designed to implement the Budget of 1986 follow a consistent pattern of economic principles that have always been the policy and strategy of the Government since it took office in September 1984.
When the Government took office on September 4, 1984, it was faced with two gigantic and enormous conflicting problems. The first, of course, was unemployment. The unemployment rate had been in excess of 13 per cent and at that time it was 11.7 per cent, the highest unemployment rate we have had in Canada since the Great Depression of the 1930s. The unemployment rate had devastated the country and continues to be a problem. The second conflicting problem the Government faced at that time was an enormous spending deficit. Not only did it face an enormous national debt load, it faced an annual federal spending deficit which was reaching at that time $36 billion per year.
In the economic statement of November 1984, in the Budget of 1985 and again in the Budget of 1986, the Minister of Finance has adopted a delicate balance of policies which are designed to try to deal with those two conflicting problems. First, the policies have been aimed at encouraging the private sector to create jobs and to solve that enormous unemployment problem. The private sector has been utilized in this strategy as the engine of economic growth. No longer are we looking to the Government to spend money and try to create these jobs on its own, because that is virtually impossible with a spending deficit that was already in the vicinity of $36 billion. The
March 13, 1986

policies are aimed at creating a climate to encourage the private sector to create the jobs necessary to get Canada growing again.
The second prong in the consistent strategy which has been followed throughout by the Minister of Finance is of course to try to put a hold on the deficit, try to stop its growth, and try to start to cut into and reduce it. Just stopping its growth was a problem in itself. At the time the Government took office in September, 1984, we did not have a deficit that was finite and identifiable with a closed end. We had policies in place at that time which were causing the deficit to continue to grow. The Minister of Finance had to find a way to stop its growth and a way to start reducing the deficit itself. That is what all the policies since the election of 1984 have been aimed at.
Last year, in the Budget of May, 1985, the Minister of Finance spelled out policies which were designed to try to encourage the private sector to create jobs. First, he allocated S900 million for job training and for job creation. In addition, he introduced other provisions which allowed for venture capital financing of small business out of pension funds and Registered Retirement Savings Plans. Aside from that, he introduced a 100 per cent tax credit on the first $2 million of qualifying research and development activity in each year. All those measures were aimed at having the private sector expand, invest and create jobs.
At the same time in last year's Budget, the Minister introduced a series of policies which were aimed at reducing the deficit. In November, 1984 and again in May, 1985, he announced major spending cuts in each and every Department of the federal Government, spending cuts which amounted in total, up to the present time and apart from anything done this year, to $5.8 billion.
Part of that effort was the commencement of a program of reducing the numbers of people in the Public Service. For a number of years the Public Service had been on an upward cycle of growth, continuous growth without any check or balance. The Minister of Finance put in place, in last year's Budget, a policy aimed at reducing the Public Service by
15,000	people, not just by eliminating jobs and putting people out on the street, but by a policy of planned attrition.

I was struck by the selective memory he displayed this morning, and by the fact that he, albeit not deliberately 1 am sure, forgot to mention in his analysis of the reduction of the deficit the measure that was introduced in the Budget which allows those who can afford it to enjoy a $500,000 capital gains tax exemption which will have a profound impact on the revenue of the Government of Canada. That measure is certainly not consistent with the goals expressed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). In fact, it is in plain contradiction of the policies which the Government has been propounding over the last year and one half.
One must also observe that the Member for York East, again I am sure inadvertently, in analysing the tax bills and putting forward their positive features, forgot about three instances of deindexation. The deindexation of senior citizens' pensions was at last repealed by the Government. The deindexation of the personal income tax deduction will increase the income tax burden on every taxpayer in Canada in the future. Finally, the deindexation of family allowances is now before the Senate and is the source of a considerable number of complaints from the women of the country. I am sure the Hon.
Member for York East will understand that in the long term, when this measure comes into full effect a few years from now, it may also cause an increase in the burden of the social budgets of municipalities and the provinces.
One must also comment on the neglect of the environment as a result of its treatment by this borrowing Bill. The thesis 1 am putting forward today is that the Government is derelict, insensitive and penny wise but pound foolish in the way it is cutting back on the Department of the environment and its programs. Let me outline the areas in which these measures are unjustified.
First, the total budget of Environment Canada in the last two years has risen by 0.5 per cent while conservative estimates show that inflation has gone up by 8 per cent in two years. Therefore, the budget of Environment Canada has been eroded by 7.5 per cent. That is the net effect on the culpability of the Government in answering the growing concern that Canadians are expressing in a variety of ways over toxic chemicals, acid rain, wildlife management, water quality and other environmental issues. According to predictions that have been made, inflation will continue and therefore erode the base of that Department. If it continues to erode at the same rate of 4 per cent, the damage a year from now will be even greater than the 7.5 per cent damage which I mentioned earlier as a result of the Government's policy in the past two years.
Let us look at the specifics of the Department of the Environment estimates for this year. For instance, we see a decline between 1984 and 1986 of some $8 million in contributions to the provinces for sewage treatment construction programs. The figure was approximately $10 million in 1984 but has dropped to $1.9 million in the estimates this year.
Let us consider the inland waters programs which includes the implementation of federal-provincial programs and the implementation of international water policy agreements. We see a cut of some $5.9 million in the capacity of the people in charge of those programs-whose number has been reduced by 14, incidentally-to do their jobs in the inland and international waters on behalf of Canadians and to implement the international agreements that we have made.
If we examine environmental protection we see a cut of $12 million between 1984 and this year. There are 25 less people in charge of that particular function within Environment Canada and the House is aware that this environmental protection section also covers the federal role in the management of PCBs, toxic chemicals and issues related to lead in gasoline, pesticides, acid rain and dioxins.
Wildlife conservation in an important program in relation to the health of Canadians in the long term because the observations that we make about wildlife will also indicate the human effect of some of the substances that are passed on to wildlife through discharges from dumps and other industrial and domestic activities. These studies may tell us about the longterm effect on humans. However, in the past two years we have seen a loss of $4.7 million to the Canadian Wildlife

The impact of that cut is not yet known to any Department, I understand, but when it is applied it will diminish the effectiveness of Environment Canada because I am sure that Department will not be spared the axe of that 2 per cent cut. It could even be a greater amount, depending on how it will be applied by Treasury Board.
In concluding this analysis on environmental cuts in the Estimates for this year, I must also draw to the attention of the House that the Department of the Environment, under the guidelines of the present Government, is also losing sight of priorities.
When one compares the priorities being adopted by the Department this year with the priorities of previous years, we see an astonishing declaration concerning acid rain. The priority of the Department this year is to implement agreements and programs that are aimed at reducing the effects of acid rain. At first sight, this may seem to be rather harmless, but reducing the effect of acid rain is totally different from the previously adopted policy priority to reduce the acid rain depositions. That priority is not in the latest Estimates.
There is a big difference between reducing acid rain depositions and reducing the effects of acid rain. Reducing the depositions means going to the source, controlling the emissions and setting specific targets and dates to ensure that they are reduced over the years. The new policy priority to reduce the effects means accepting the level of acid rain depositions or emissions in the environment and trying to cure the effects of these depositions. This means that these priorities are shifting attention from controlling the emissions at the source to treating the depositions and their effects on the environment. I submit that this is a very serious shift in policy and I cannot understand why all of the efforts that so far have been aimed and focused on prevention should suddenly be abandoned, by virtue of this priority as stated in the Estimates, and replaced by a policy to reduce the effects. I cannot express it any other way than to say that this shift in policy disturbs me profoundly and I cannot understand how or why it has happened.
In order to bring to your attention the fact that Environment Canada is losing sight of its priorities, let me raise another point. This year the water quality in the Great Lakes Basin, Lake Ontario and the other Great Lakes is not listed as a priority. There is no reference to the St. Clair River or to the Niagara River. That is a serious omission if one considers that the concerns of Canadians who live along the St. Clair and Niagara Rivers are at an all-time high. Second, we must consider the fact that we have an international obligation to discharge, by virtue of the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. Here, again, for the life of me, I cannot understand the Government's position with the upsurge of public interest and concern and with the hundreds of questions which have been asked in this House during Question Period by Members of all Parties, including the Hon. Member for York East, who has been a tower of strength in this debate. It just defeats my

ability to understand why these priorities do not emerge in the Estimates of Environment Canada in 1986-87.
What we are witnessing here is the Government losing sight of priorities as expressed in the Estimates. We have witnessed over the years 1984 to 1986 a number of cuts applied to Environment Canada. In addition to that, the purchasing power of that Department is losing ground rapidly in relation to inflation. That is not fair, it is not desirable, and it is not in the public interest.
In his Budget, the Minister of Finance included a measure whereby there would be a three-year tax write-off on wind energy equipment. That raised a lot of questions because one wonders why there would be just a measure to favour wind energy equipment. I am sure there is a very good reason for it, and that there are people who will, hopefully, take advantage of it. But there is nothing for other renewable sources of energy like solar energy biomass, and so on. This narrow approach to renewable sources of energy is a puzzle.
In analysing the measures which should have been introduced by the Minister of Finance, but which were not, in relation to environmental issues which are emerging with greater frequency and importance, one wonders why the Minister of Finance did not provide, in the light of what is happening on the St. Clair and Niagara Rivers, some measures for an accelerated tax write-off which would be applied on pollution abatement equipment and which would give the industries along the St. Clair and Niagara Rivers, an incentive to clean up, so to speak, their act. Evidently, these are old fashioned, outdated, operations. The equipment is getting old. The incidence of accidents and spills are becoming more and more frequent. There are measures available to the Minister of Finance to encourage and entice the industries which are engaged in these operations every day to do their part and to clean up their act. I was looking forward to finding some of those measures in the Budget, but they were not there.
Another initiative which the Minister of Finance will sooner or later have to take into account and apply in his Budget is a change in the tax structures on gasoline. You have heard me before, Mr. Speaker, express my view about the necessity of changing our design of the taxes as they apply to leaded and unleaded gasoline so that the price at the pump will be equal for both. The revenue to the Government would remain the same but the demand for unleaded would be greater than now and the demand for leaded would be less. In doing so, we in North America would be pioneering, although not globally, a measure which was introduced in Denmark and Austria. The public buys at the pump either leaded or unleaded gasoline at the same price. That would once and for all do away with the practice of misfueling. We would also reduce the amount of lead in the air and on the ground which, as you know, Mr. Speaker, harms the health of humans, particularly children. In the Budget there was no reference, unfortunately, to reinstating the Guelph Toxicology Centre. We in this House, from all Parties, who are engaged in matters which relate to water quality, know how important it is to maintain the momentum of our research on toxicology, and particularly on the impact of certain substances in water. Yet, a measure which was announced in 1983-84, to become a reality in 1984-85, has been wiped out. I wonder sometimes about the Government because that is not the way to protect the public interests, by neglecting the basics which relate to public health. We should develop the instruments which will put to work the scientists we have and prevent them from leaving Canada to go abroad, enticed by other opportunities. This Government can provide them with opportunities at home in the field of research in which they are competent and for which there is a future and a necessity for the protection of the health of Canadians. I despair sometimes about this lack of sense of direction on the part of this Progressive Conservative Government.
I would like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the fact that in the Budget-and I do hope the Government will pay attention to this at the next opportunity-there is no attention being paid to the plight of municipalities to modernize sewers, to separate where necessary their sewer systems. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday you will recall, on the eve of International Women's Day, Conservative Members ignored the agreement to put up speakers which had been arranged with other Parties and therefore closed debate on the Budget. This was done before I was allowed to speak on the impact of the Budget on Canadian women. I do not recall hearing any Conservative speaker mentioning the impact of the Budget on Canadian women. That is one of the things on which I want to concentrate my remarks today. I might say that the Budget was a typical act of discrimination.
It is difficult to determine just what the Government intends to do with the $22.6 billion it wants authorization to borrow under Bill C-99. I personally would be much happier to support this Bill if I thought the money would go toward positive measures that would improve the lot of ordinary Canadians, particularly Canadian women, children and young people. Unfortunately, because of the Budget which we have been studying and about which we are very concerned, we know that the government measures are very negative measures. We know that these funds will be used largely for those same negative measures.
I would like to bring to the attention of the House, and particularly Conservative Members, the fact that over the last month there has been the greatest surge of short-term borrowing in the history of Canada. This was concurrent with the time the Budget was introduced and was becoming known to Canadians and the international community. Of course, this
happened largely because the Government had to put billions of dollars, I assume, into propping up the Canadian dollar. Along with that, we were paying and will continue to pay increased interest on the amount of money that was going to prop up the Canadian dollar.
This dramatic drop in the value of the dollar over the past month was directly related to the lack of confidence in the Government and its Budget. Not only does it cost us more in interest rates because of that lack of confidence, we calculated that each Canadian family would pay an average of $100 per year in increased food costs, something about which we do not always think. This borrowing Bill repeats the negative philosophy and negative use of borrowed funds which are costing us all much more in interest.
Of course, women share in the lack of confidence in the Government which was reflected by the drop in the dollar. There was no mention in the Budget of women at all, and certainly there was no reference to the very strong statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in Halifax at the First Ministers' Conference. At that time he said that all Governments must give priority to economic equality for women. The Government makes no mention of this when it gets down to doing something in the way of a Budget. There was nothing in the Budget designed to deal with the inequities for women and other minority groups that must be redressed.
As I said, women were not mentioned at all in the Budget. On the other hand, when looking at the Budget closely, we realize that it adds another layer of financial burden on women. Women are already the poorest of our citizens and still earn just 63 cents on the dollar. Women carry double work-loads at home and in the workplace. As I mentioned yesterday, farm women often carry three heavy work-loads while there is no day care for their children. Women are the last hired and the first fired, particularly if they happen to work for the federal Government. Women are being pushed further into part-time, low-paid jobs that are not unionized and do not have benefits, or they are being forced to go on unemployment insurance. This is as a result of the policies of the Government, which is pushing for even more privatization and deregulation and for more government cut-backs in public services.
As I mentioned earlier when I spoke to one of my colleagues, we are very concerned about the Budget from an international point of view and how it will affect our pride in Canada's role in the world. The Budget cuts back on international aid, and this has a tremendous impact, particularly on women and children in developing countries. These women and children are indeed going to be condemned to die in many cases as a result of Budget cuts.
Before I return to the particular parts of this Budget about which I am concerned, and about which Canadian women are becoming increasingly concerned, I would like to mention a few other points. As we have said over and over again, the average family is grossly and unfairly taxed, to the tune of something over $1,300 in additional taxes over the last two years. On the other hand, wealthy families continue to benefit
March 13, 1986

from the capital gains tax exemptions and there is nothing at all in the Budget to indicate that there has been real tax reforms such as those we have advocated.
As a British Columbia, I would like to say that I am very concerned. The Conservative Budget is a disaster for British Columbia. We need more jobs, not just more cuts and taxes on top of what we already have in the way of British Columbia restraint programs. Direct federal spending on job creation will be cut by an additional $100 million this year.
In many parts of B.C. unemployment continues to be as high, if not higher than in the maritime provinces. For example, unemployment in Victoria, the capital city of British Columbia, is the highest in Canada. It is over 16 per cent. I should like to warn the Conservatives in the Government that the Government of British Columbia practised the restraint the present Conservative Government is imposing federally, and it has resulted in 16 per cent unemployment in Victoria. No special initiatives were taken in the Budget to create new jobs in British Columbia.
We have heard many suggestions from New Democrats respecting concrete job proposals; investment in community development, enhancement of the forest and fishery resources, and reform of taxes to help pay for many things. Recently I received a telegram from a group in British Columbia, the Mothers Action Committee, which indicated that hundreds of thousands of Canadian women are struggle daily under terrible conditions of poverty to survive and raise children, and that deliberate Government policies make the rich richer and oppress women. They want money for child care, pensions for homemakers, reindexing of the family allowance and fair pay for their work. Of course the Budget and Government policies will do just the opposite for women. The tremendous tax load of over $1,300, which I mentioned, will have a much greater or disproportionate impact upon women. In effect, it will push more women and their children into poverty; there is no question about it.
The cuts to Public Service jobs have already affected women disproportionately. 1 have been told that in the translation department, for example, 63 per cent of the lay-offs were women, yet only 52 per cent of the staff are women. In the fisheries Department, many more women were let go, yet there are very few women employed in that Department. Over-all cuts to certain Government Departments will also affect women's jobs and services to women. For example, the Budget shows that $4.82 billion, a lot of money, will be cut from the Department of National Health and Welfare over the next four years. From where will it be cut? We know where it will be cut. It will be cuts in family benefits and in programs such as Planned Parenthood, the National Clearing House on Family Violence and non-statutory services. The Minister mentioned that discretionary funding would be at risk. It will be cuts to women's organizations and community non-governmental organizations which are already under funded. We have also learned, from the point of view of the Nielsen task
Borrowing Authority Act
force, that a cut of $9 million is proposed from Secretary of State women's programs. That is unforgiveable and intolerable.
The Budget also cut employment training programs which will have a great impact upon women. In 1984 women only had about 14 per cent of the training spaces. I raised this matter, along with a number of issues, with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) last week. There will also be a cut of over $100 million from the Canadian Jobs Strategy, at a time when we need more money for job strategy, particularly for women. Now the Nielsen task force is advocating more cuts.
The Government brags about helping those in need. I find that to be unforgiveable on the part of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). It is bad enough that he does these things, but he tries to fool people, particularly those who are hurting and have no power to fight back. It is quite unforgiveable. He says that he is designing programs to help those in greatest need, but let us look at the actual facts.
The National Council of Welfare figures prove that the impact of the Conservative Budget, without even looking at the impact of the sales taxes, will result in the lowering of the disposable income of a family which is at three-quarters of the poverty level-a very poor family-by $118, while an upper income earner who receives over $100,000 will gain $422. The poor family loses $118, plus the sales tax increases which will be imposed, while the high income earner gains $422 plus tax benefits. How can one possibly say that it helps those in greatest need?
Let us look at the so-called child tax credit and the family allowance which have both been deindexed. The value is being eroded. The terminology is being changed. We no longer talk about universality; we talk about universal access. We know that means an erosion of universal family programs. The refundable tax credit will not cover last year's sales tax increases, much less compensate families for the loss of indexation on family benefits. It also penalizes single mothers who do not receive the extra $ 100 for a spouse.
The Government has allocated $100 million per year to new employment initiatives for social assistance recipients. I caution the Government. It should make sure that it consults with community people, including those from low-income organizations, on how the money should be used. We could really get into a bind if we are not careful here. We do not want punitive work for welfare measures as the Nielsen task force recommends for native people. If women on welfare are to take advantage of job opportunities, they must have training and child care, and there is nothing in the Budget in that regard. I hope that some of the new funding will go toward funding self-help programs and toward community development in low-income communities, which will provide double benefits in terms of improving community support services as well as providing paycheques.
I am extremely disappointed, as are Canadian women and men, particularly those who are parents, that the Government completely ignored the very urgent need for federal funding to

March 13, 1986
Borrowing Authority Act
begin to upgrade and expand many forms of child care. We need money now, according to the Cooke report which was tabled last week, to begin to upgrade existing services so that children are not placed at risk and many working parents at least begin to feel that there is some licensed care in communities.
The proposal of Katie Cooke was a very conservative one. It was far too conservative, from my point of view, but it made clear that the federal Government must put some good-faith federal grants into the system this year so that we can begin to build toward a much more comprehensive child care service in all communities in the future. Only 13 per cent of our families are so-called traditional families now. Eighty-seven per cent are families with two parents working, and in the case of 10 per cent of them they are families headed by women. We have a whole new society in Canada. The Conservative Government, especially the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), has to begin to accept reality. Fifty-two per cent of the mothers of infants are in the workforce and they do not have care for their children. Over the past eight years there has been a 60 per cent increase in the numbers of families that need child care. I could go on and on.
In 1984, there were almost two million children who needed care and we had only 171,000 licensed spaces for them. We have to begin to act on this. Even from an economic point of view, I hope Conservative Members realize that many mothers have to work. If they do not work there will be more poor families on welfare. The cost of investing in day care is not only essential to children, but it will also save both social costs and costs for women who would otherwise remain on welfare all their lives.
In conclusion, we are very disappointed, in fact very crushed by the federal Budget, particularly the lack of any recognition of the need for women to achieve equality and for low-income families to have the opportunities they deserve, which is their right in a rich country like Canada. We have to plan for economic equality. The Government is pushing people backward and is particularly penalizing women and children.

subtopic: REACTION OF INTEREST GROUPS
REACTION OF INTEREST GROUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the great Canadian tragedy is that once a Government program is in place it develops a constituency, which either continues to support it on principle or, worse, depends on it in practice. The dependency becomes addictive. The expenditures become entrenched.
The original purpose of the program is lost as the beneficiaries come to view the program not as a privilege but rather as a right. The tabling of the report of the Task Force on Program Review represents a giant step on the road to more efficient government. Yet already, Mr. Speaker, we are hearing howls of anguish from the interest groups vehemently denouncing any possible reduction or diminution of what they view as their particular entitlement.
I urge all Members carefully and objectively to consider the various recommendations put forward by this non-partisan public and private sector task force.
Canadians have a right to expect government that serves their needs at a reasonable cost.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on some of the remarks of the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) and determine whether she agrees with my observations on the Conservative Government's current policy for members of the Armed Forces. The Government has eliminated the possibility for retiring members of the Canadian Armed Forces to obtain unemployment insurance. This is essentially changing the game plan in the middle of the game for these people who have served their country for many years. They have contributed to the unemployment insurance program for from 20 to 30 years. That insurance has been calculated as part of their pension to assist them in making the transition from their jobs to a much diminished income. They have actually been put out of the Armed Forces, because they do not have any choice whether or not they will leave.
This hits them at a time in life when their family expenses are extremely high. Their children are in their late teens and require support for post-secondary education. Children need much financial assistance just before they become adults. This is one of the most devious and under-handed things that has been done to members of the Canadian Armed Forces.
In addition, there are two other small things which the Government has done in the same vein. It has attempted to partially deindex pensions of retired members of the Armed Forces. The Government insists that those members who find jobs to help themselves over this very difficult transition pay unemployment insurance premiums, but that they can never collect unemployment insurance.
I would like to hear the comments of the Member for Vancouver East on this. Does she agree with me that the Conservative Government has been extremely hard-handed with members of the Armed Forces in this matter?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is at least the fifteenth time I have spoken on borrowing authority Bills since I was elected in 1979, and returned to the House as the Member for Mississauga South. speechtext:
The fiscal plan produced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) only takes into account the history back to the 1977-78 year with respect to national accounts, financial requirements and the budgetary deficit. Looking that over, you can note the continual increase for every year, until the 1984-85, of the percentage of Gross National Product committed to paying the cost of borrowing. For the first time we are able to reduce the amount required to be borrowed from 6.3 per cent of the Gross National Product to 4.6 per cent of the Gross National Product. That truly is a remarkable change.
It is that kind of activity, as we take hold of this country and turn it around, that again will give this country hope for the future, for ourselves, for our children and for our grandchildren. The last two decades have been plagued with Governments going to the well to pay current bills, using a Chargex
card to run the country, to buy the groceries. We have not been paying our way. We have been borrowing on the future of the country without any sense of responsibility. This has changed.
If you take a look at the projections in the Budget Papers you will see that the requirement to borrow goes down next year to $17.6 billion, and eventually, even on the most pessimistic basis, to no more than $11 billion.
I call Mr. Wilson the pessimistic Minister of Finance because his projections are all pessimistic. While last year he felt we would need the deficit we had, indeed, we will probably wind up spending far less than projected, despite the problems we had with banks in western Canada.
What is happening is that our Minister of Finance has taken a look at the country and has said: "Well, we can at least do this, and that is our Budget". I tell you that this Budget, in terms of deficits, in terms of projections, in terms of costs, is pessimistic. We are going to do better than we are forecasting. More of that later.
Let us get to some figures. The Minister of Finance says that growth will only be 2.7 per cent in the next five years until 1990-91. He also says that growth last year was only 4.5 per cent. In fact it was 4.9 per cent. Nobody has forecast growth over the next five years to be as little as 2.7 per cent. Indeed, if you ask the Royal Bank of Canada, they say we are pessimistic. If you ask Data Resources, we are pessimistic. If you ask Informetrica we are pessimistic. The growth projections in the Budget are pessimistic.
Let us consider the oil prices. The Opposition said that the price of oil stated by the Minister of Finance in his Budget was wrong and that his deficit projections would be far off the mark. The fact is that the Economic Council of Canada has said that the Gross National Product will increase, employment will increase and inflation will decrease if oil prices fall. That is all good news. The Minister of Finance projects the price of oil to be $22.50 a barrel. At $15 a barrel our year will be even better than predicted.
The Minister pointed out that we had a small flip in interest rates which pushed them up for a short term in order to protect our currency. However, interests rates are falling dramatically and will fall even further with the decline in the price of oil. Members of the House will note that on Monday the Government of the United States was able to borrow its treasury bill money at 6.5 per cent. Members will also know that on a 90-day basis the Eurodollar rate is less than 7.5 per cent, the LIBOR rate is less than 7.5 per cent and that our interest rates dropped 105 bases points today. I suggest that the projection of 9.5 per cent for interest rates in the fiscal year commencing April 1 is pessimistic because, with any performance at all that follows the United States, Germany or Japan, our interest rates will be dramatically lower than those forecast by the Minister of Finance. Therefore, it may not be necessary to call upon the borrowing authority required here.
March 13, 1986

The budgeted borrowing authority is $22.6 billion. I suspect that we will not borrow the total amount which we authorized last year, nor borrow all the money that is authorized in this Bill. I am optimistic. It is the first time I have been able to come to the House, since 1979, and say that we are doing a good job in coming to grips with the problems of the country.
It distresses me to see the Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) suggest we are only optimistic when we talk to foreign Governments. Let me tell her that we are optimistic when we talk to Canadians and she should be as optimistic because she should be promoting Canada instead of being negative. We could make Canada grow while solving our problems. That is the attitude that should be taken by Members opposite. That is the kind of attitude Canadians expect and that is the kind of attitude we should have. I am proud that our Government and our foreign offices throughout the world are displaying that attitude.
In his speech last night the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) asked investors to look at Canada closely for business opportunities. It is that kind of speech which we ought to be giving in selling our nation and promoting the possibilities that exist in our great land.
We have heard numerous comments about exchange rates. Let me expand on that for a moment. I do not agree with the use of interest rates to influence the exchange policy of the country. Frankly, I do not always agree with the Minister of Finance, and I profoundly disagree with this particular policy produced by the Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Bank of Canada. In my view, exchange rates are determined by an active and aggressive market, buying and selling currency.
Our trading activity in the market-place with the United States is truly amazing. Indeed, we do well over $100 billion worth of trade with that country, which means the buying, selling and dealing in American exchange is truly phenomenal.
While speculation takes place, we should question why we have an exchange rate for our currency that perhaps is less than what it should actually indicate when we consider the price of goods and services as offered in the market-place. Members will know that the Economic Council of Canada, in making comparisons between goods for sale in New York State and Ontario, has indicated that the Canadian dollar should perhaps be worth 80 cents, on a market price for goods basis, in comparison to the American dollar. I believe that the Economic Council is right.
Some may ask why our exchange rate may drop below 70 cents, certainly not a strong and active rate. The reason is a phenomenon that has not existed in this country until now, and which some people policing our exchange rate have not recognized. That phenomenon is prosperity. There is an economic boom in this country, primarily in Ontario and Quebec. Unfortunately, that boom has not spread throughout the country because such a boom throughout the country would have been better for everyone. Huge regional disparities are detrimental to our economic plan, because we have to maintain certain programs in some parts of the country, yet they may not be
Borrowing Authority Act
necessary in other areas and could become anti-productive. Currently there is a strong boom in southern Ontario and certainly in Quebec. For the first time there are areas in this country where there is, in fact, over-employment. Businessmen are calling constituency offices asking why the Government does not bring in immigrants. They want to know why they cannot yet help when the Government is paying out unemployment insurance. These businessmen are prepared to offer from $8 to $12 an hour.
What effect does this have on the exchange rate front? For example, when Canadians are prosperous they go south in the winter. That affects our exchange because those Canadians convert Canadian dollars into American dollars. Canadians also import more goods when they are prosperous. While we still have a massive trade surplus, our imports are rising as a proportion of trade activity and this increase in imported goods effects our exchange rates.
Finally, as Canadian companies become more prosperous and increase their trade with the United States they have a dramatic increase in inventory in the United States. These companies are increasing their export financing and becoming more active in other countries. Last weekend, three of my constituents told me that their companies were becoming more involved in the United States. One is a computer organized company that was developed in Toronto and carries on research and development. It has had to open branch offices in New York and Los Angeles in order to get business. In order to open those offices and develop its programming it must remove money from Canada. However, it returns profits to Canada which benefits our country.
Another constituent is involved in a foreign exchange banking operation. That operation bought out the American company and is moving the head office from New York to Toronto. What does that do? It means that Canadian dollars have gone out to buy up that company, and that is good for Canada, but, unfortunately, that affects our foreign exchange. I have another situation in a manufacturing operation partly because of the problems we have with liability insurance. The Canadian manufacturer has had to open an American plant so there can be partial manufacturing done down there. In that way it will solve some of the tariff problems, the buy-Ameri-can problems, the trade problems we still have with the United States and, in fact, the insurance problem. Again, that is an outflow of cash and investment but it is a profitable investment for Canada. It is good for Canada and for Canadian employment.
All of this prosperity affects the trade value for our dollar and we should not be upset with it. The market-place operates the way the market-place ought to operate. It is the discipline of the market-place and we cannot change it by jigabooing around with interest rates.

A lot of times we hear that foreigners are going to bring money into our country to develop business. That is not what we are looking for in Toronto. We are not looking for debt money. We are looking for equity money and new ideas. Businessmen do not just invest money, they invest ideas. When one has an idea or a capacity as a developer, or whatever, and one goes to a foreign country, one takes one's ideas and some money, but mostly the money is borrowed in that foreign country. That is how our developers who have built the office buildings in Houston, Los Angeles and New York and who have developed the subdivisions in Florida, have operated. That is how they have done it. That is our export of services. What we in Toronto are trying to do is to attract people who have the ideas and some of the up-front capital and they can borrow more money in Canada if they wish because Canada has lots of capital. Canada does not need just money, it needs ideas, entrepreneurship and new growth, and we will get that in a trade operation such as is in Toronto right now.
If our people are out doing things, that is good for Canada and if we attract new business into Canada which will make use of Canada's capital, that is all right. We need the new business and the growth. We need the new entrepreneurship. That's how it works.
I would like to speak for a moment about the amount of our debt and the way the debt is held. At the present time, a great deal of our debt is held in what I call "current account" debt, that is, in Canada savings bonds and in Treasury bills. Indeed, about 65 per cent to 70 per cent of our debt is held in that fashion. One of the problems of holding debt in that fashion is the kind of problem the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) faced two, three or four weeks ago when in order to prevent people from cashing Canada savings bonds, he was forced to increase the interest rates on them for a short-term period.
Something we have to do in the management of the national debt is to convert more of that debt into more long-term debt. We must, therefore, as this year goes by, rely less and less upon Canada savings bonds for our debt pattern and more and more on long-term debt instruments. Second, we have to take a look at the whole question of T-bills and stop borrowing as much as we are on T-bills. Some of those people with those high interest T-bill accounts in Canada Trust had better understand that they should load up in a hurry because interest rates are going to drop as we make this economy grow. The Budget is pessimistic in terms of our debt requirement. The Nielsen task force report with its ideas, the Forget Commission which will probably revamp and cut down on the cost of the unemployment insurance scheme, and other things which are going on, will make Canada grow again and grow
well. I am happy to speak on this borrowing Bill because for the first time we have turned the economy around.

The point is that the people living below that poverty line ought not to be taxed. This point was made by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) last week when he pointed out that Members on all sides of the House know that, if we were to be fair, no person living in poverty would be pushed further into poverty by being made to pay taxes when there are people in the country who pay no taxes at all because they are rich enough to hire lawyers and accountants to fiddle their reports.
Countries such as Scandinavia have ensured that people who live in poverty pay no taxes. If they can do it, we can do it here. Three decades ago individuals and corporations each paid about half of the income taxes which were collected. After the new Budget individuals will pay 80 per cent and corporations will pay only 20 per cent. That is grossly unfair. In fact, the new Budget has imposed upon working people rates of taxation 10 times higher than those imposed upon corporations. The 3 per cent surtax, the 1 per cent sales increase and the other sales taxes that the Government has imposed will take about $350 per year extra over and beyond the Government's previous $1,000 bite, $350 per year extra for every working family, whereas for the corporations there is a continuation of $500,000 capital gains tax-and for a married couple that is a $1 million. There is no return to the 1981 marginal rates, which charge the rich a higher rate of their income than they charge the poor, and there is no bringing in of a tax expenditure account so that the public can see how much goes to rich individuals and to corporations through the Government's tax expenditures, that is to say through the taxes they owe that the Government remits to them for reasons that are never fully examined in the actual practice.
There are cuts in badly-needed services to the people of Canada. Regional, industrial expansion will be cut by $2 billion. The service to unemployed people, including services for which they have paid by their contributions will be cut by $1.75 billion. Assistance to farmers who are going broke and out of business at a record rate not equalled since the Depression days will be cut by half a billion. Health and Welfare will be cut by $4 billion. Transport, particularly rail and road transport, the sort used by the majority of this country, the poor people, the low-income and low middle-income people in this country, that will be cut by over $3.5 billion.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) is in the House. I hope he will relay my remarks to some of his colleagues.
With respect to this borrowing authority, I urge the Government to amend the Bill next Monday to increase its borrowing by at least $1 billion. Let me explain why. The Government is deluding itself if it believes it can rely on the private sector to provide essential public and social needs at minimum or no profit. It never has happened and never will.
That is why Governments at all levels must intervene to provide those essential public services and facilities at cost.
Let me say at the outset that I and my Party are fully in favour of efficiency in the administration of Government programs and obtaining full value for every tax dollar spent. However, most of what the Government borrows is used to pay interest charges to banks, investors and foreign lenders. I want us to return to borrowing for those things that are self-liquidating, constructive debts that fulfil the needs of the nation.
Perhaps Hon. Members watched the television news in the past two days and The Journal last night on the CBC. If so, they saw concrete evidence of what is happening. In every city of this country there is a waiting list as long as your arm for senior citizen housing, co-op housing, municipal housing, homes for the aged sponsored by church and volunteer agencies, chronic care beds and hospital beds. I had an experience today in the emergency wing of a hospital in this city. There are not enough beds. There are people filling chronic care beds in hospitals. We need a massive investment in this area by
federal, provincial and municipal Governments. Even if it requires borrowing for construction of those facilities, and to purchase the equipment needed, it will put tens of thousands to work and the debt will be self-liquidating. The amount of money which could be collected from income taxes, sales taxes and other kinds of revenues available to the three levels of Government could retire those borrowings in one or two years. That is a positive and constructive kind of deficit.
This nation needs the modernization and expansion of those areas. The construction industry alone affects the entire economy. The forest industry, the steel industry, those who manufacture appliances, carpets and drapes, those who install wiring and plumbing as well as those who do the construction of the buildings, are all put to work and all pay taxes. I would like to urge the Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing to ask his colleagues for an additional $1 billion of borrowing in the coming year, in a joint effort with other levels of Government and with church and volunteer organizations, to give us what we are sadly lacking. There is no excuse for allowing people to sit in a wheelchair in an emergency wing for an entire day and then lie in a bed in an emergency room for three days waiting for a hospital bed. There are people who are chronically ill, who do not require full-time hospital attention, but do require a chronic care bed. There is a chain of terrible treatment and behaviour, and I believe every Hon. Member of this House of every political Party could justify borrowing for that kind of investment if this nation is going to be a little more decent, civilized and humane.
We have to use sound business sense in what we borrow money for. We should have borrowings which are self-liquidating rather than just dead weight in a vicious circle of interest upon interest paid to those who have not contributed anything. That is what is needed. I hope that the Government will amend its own Bill because I cannot do so, nor can my Party.
If there are any borrowings unused from the previous year in excess of $2 billion, the Government should use it for the kinds of things I have just mentioned. We had a debate on Wednesday, an Opposition Day, about youth and youth employment. With another $1 billion worth of borrowing over a five-year period we could put a quarter of a million people, most of them young, to work doing nothing more than cleaning up our air and water. That is an investment. Anyone who sits in this place and thinks for one moment that the private sector will do that on its own, by reducing its profits, is dreaming in technicolour. It cannot and will not do it because of the bottom line syndrome: maximize profit, and the benefits to the shareholders take priority over the welfare and good order of this nation. That is why Governments must intervene. Of course, we can try to persuade the private sector to join in and make their fair share of contribution even if it means some shareholders will have to take 25 cents or a dollar less in dividends on their shares for a year or two. We could pay off our deficit in a much shorter period of time and the private sector should be challenged to do that.

I want to say to my colleagues in the Conservative Party that I made the same kind of argument to Ministers of Finance in previous Liberal Governments.
I want to appeal to the Minister in charge of Canada Mortgage and Housing. If he has any weight and muscle in his Cabinet, he will bring in an amendment to the borrowing authority Bill next Monday for an additional $1 billion to put into place the items I have just mentioned.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ENTERTAINMENT INDUSTRY SUGGESTED COMMITTEE STUDY OF STANDARDS FOR RATING AND LABELLING
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs be empowered to study the question of consumer standards for rating and labelling in the entertainment industry, particularly with respect to videos, records, cassette tapes and compact discs, and that in undertaking this study, the committee focus on the question of sexually explicit lyrics and the negative moral effect this may be having on the youth of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on December 3 of last year I had the occasion to make a statement in the House decrying the violent and sexually explicit lyrics in certain types of today's music, music which is directed not so much at the population at large but rather at the most impressionable and vulnerable of our population-the teens and preteens. As I mentioned in my statement, this had been brought to my attention by the New Brunswick Federation of Home and School Associations.
Frankly, as I had to admit at that time, I had not been paying attention to the music and was, therefore, ignoring the words, the words with their almost subliminal message of torture, degradation, rape, rebellion and even suicide. Thankfully, others had been listening, people from coast to coast, parents, teachers, church groups and students who have written to me and who have said quite simply to the recording and video industry and to the provincial and federal representatives: "Enough is enough".
This is not a new issue in North America. 1 am not crusading for a new cause, a new platform to introduce censorship of any kind. I recognize not just the difficulty but the futility in that, an attempt by anyone to deny anyone what they perceive to be their legitimate rights and freedoms. This issue has been raised before by a number of organizations. Most noticeably and most recently it has been raised by a group of Washington wives of U.S. Congressmen and Senators who have organized themselves into the Parents Music Resource Centre.
What is it that they want? What is it that the New Brunswick federation wants? It wants the recording industry to start policing itself with the same standards along the lines of the film industry's rating system. An industry which will not police itself will be policed. It will be regulated to some degree if it flauts the mores of a society or of a country.
A disc jockey called me in December and told me he had made a point of listening to the words, to the message, of some of the recordings he had been playing for months and months, artists to which I had objected. He admitted quite frankly that he was absolutely shocked at what he had been playing and would therefore refuse to ever play them again. This was not a

March 13, 1986
Entertainment Industry
radio station in a small rural area but, indeed, a radio station in a rather large urban centre.
Whether by coincidence or by design, on December 3, 1985, the same day I brought this matter up in the House originally, the Canadian Recording Industry Association announced new guidelines for its members on the subject of explicit lyrics in sound recordings. The President of the Association, Mr. Brian Robertson, said that the guidelines which had been accepted by all its members will recommend that future recordings, where contractually admissible and that in the opinion of the record company contain explicit language or lyrics, will carry the inscription: "Explicit Lyrics-Parental Guidance Advisory"
This is a responsible step. 1 applaud the association for taking it. However, there are still questions which must be asked, questions which must be answered. In the association's press release it was stated that its research had shown that the number of records that might fall under the category requiring a warning label was less than 1 per cent of the recordings released. One would ask: What number of that 1 per cent would be covered by the caveat "contractually permissible"?
Of course, it is not just the recording industry itself which must be brought into perspective here. What of the radio stations which will continue to play these records with the objectionable lyrics warning or not? Indeed, one could well ask: What is the air time of these records which make up less than I per cent of the recording industry? Also, and unfortunately so, many of the recording artists who have record sales of several million and fall into this category of sexually explicit music record for companies which do not belong to the Canadian Recording Association.
When we speak of the right of self-expression, the right to express oneself is not always absolute. It is generally acknowledged that some forms of regulation are appropriate and necessary in a democratic society. Other people have a correlative right not to be exposed to certain types of expression if they do not wish to be so exposed. Certain vulnerable members of society, such as children, should be shielded from some types of expression. These limitations on expression are particularly important with respect to certain recorded forms of entertainment such as video cassettes, discs and records. They can be purchased without a full knowledge of their contents. The implication of the potentially wide distribution of such materials was recently reviewed by the Special Committee on Pornography and Prostitution, the Fraser Committee. The report of that committee described the concerns that had been expressed to it on video recordings thus:
There was strong support at the public hearings for review and classification schemes applicable to video recording sold or rented for private use. The major concern of advocates of this proposal was for the young people. Worried about the kinds of violence, degradation and explicit sex which children might be seeing on videotapes parents and others were concerned that they now have almost no effective way of monitoring children's viewing.
We were told that the covers and advertising of videotapes often do not give accurate clues about the nature of the film. The merchants who rent tapes may not be as vigilant as many would hope in ensuring that young people avoid the worst material. Even where the retailer is watchful, young people may be getting
videotapes in the same way that they traditionally got liquor or cigarettes: having an older youth obtain supplies for younger peers.
The ease with which videotapes can be duplicated means that they will be widely and readily accessible. Outlets have proliferated, with videotapes being available anywhere from the largest department store to the corner gas station to the specialized video outlet, be it an adult video club or a neighbourhood family store. Video recorders are now reasonably widely available in private homes across Canada and home viewing means a consumption of the materials can take place in private. For many young people this means away from parental supervision.
The committee found real merit in having a regulatory scheme for sold or rented video recordings. The scheme would include only classification of tapes and their clear designation but not prohibition of sale or deletions. Such prohibition would be reserved for only the most seriously offensive films under the criminal obscenity standard. Accordingly, the Fraser Committee recommended that each province should establish a system of review and classification for video recordings.
The rationale for classification of video recordings would be equally applicable to audio recording. First, there is the concern that people may be offended by the contents of certain recordings of which they have no warning. Further, there is the perception that young people may be harmed by some types of video or audio entertainment. There is the general harmful effect that the depiction of explicit violence or sex is said to have in the development of those who are not sufficiently mature to deal with such forms of stimulus. Unregulated access to materials by children could seriously impair proper socialization and a growth of responsible attitudes and behaviour. Moreover, there is the more disturbing contention that some recordings have the potential to cause direct harm and that already some youth have reacted in a violent fashion to the images and ideas to which they have been exposed as a result of the indiscriminate distribution of such materials.
If these concerns have substance, it is surely arguable that review, classification and labelling of recorded materials is not an over-reaction. This would seem to be one area in which a careful review by the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee of the effect of the broad distribution of video and audio recording could indeed be of use. Such a study could focus the attention of the public and legislators on the specific issue of recorded entertainment and serve to investigage and analyse the supposed harms that flow from its distribution, particularly among youth.
Classification of film is not something that is new in Canada. Eight provinces already have film classification boards which rate films and which, in some cases, have the power to order deletion or forbid the exhibition of films. The two remaining provinces rely on the findings of the boards of other provinces. The power of these boards, however, extends only to films being shown publicly in theatres. Constitutionally, the regulation of such exhibition is considered to be within
March 13, 1986

provincial competence over matters of a local or private nature in the province and the Supreme Court of Canada has upheld the exercise of that power.
It seems clear that the extension of a classification system to the distribution of recorded material for private use would similarly be within provincial competence. This is not to say, however, that it is not possible for the federal Government to become involved in the matter, principally through the use of the criminal law power.
The classification of privately used video and audio material is becoming a significant issue in other jurisdictions as well as in Canada. As I mentioned earlier, in the United States this issue has also been raised by a number of groups and organizations. A subcommittee of the U.S. Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee recently held hearings into a proposal to require the labelling of phonograph recordings with warnings as to explicit lyrics or certain types of subject matter dealt with in the recording. Witnesses who had supported the proposal acknowledged that popular music has always been disapproved of by other generations but submitted that recently such music has undergone a serious shift in emphasis into so-called porn rock, the glorification of such things as sado-masochism, incest, bondage, indiscriminate killing and, as I have already mentioned, suicide.
Similar concerns have been expressed with respect to video presentations of popular music. Some witnesses urged legislation on that matter while others submit that self-regulation may be possible and that the recording industry should start policing itself along the lines of the film industry's rating system. For example, it could establish a voluntary rating system such as the Motion Picture Association of America has with respect to film.
Two Canadian provinces have taken steps to classify video recordings. In Nova Scotia, the province's Amusements Authority Board has been empowered, pursuant to the Theatres and Amusements Act, to regulate film exhanges, retail outlets which sell, lease, lend, exchange or distribute films to the public. Such exchanges must be licensed before they are permitted to operate. In addition, every video film including video cassettes, video discs and video tapes must be marked with a classification assigned to it by the board both on the container in which it is kept and on any container used for display purposes. That classification can be "general", "adult" or "restricted". The regulation contemplates that some video films may be distributed without having been classified and requires such video films to be marked "unclassified".
Theoretically, through the use of the criminal law power, the federal Government could impose a national system of review and classification of recorded material. However, this would involve significant costs and could serve to alienate the provinces. The federal Government is not limited to a direct role in this area.
An airing of these issues at the national level could serve to encourage the development of review and classification systems across the country. It could also lead to the development of minimum standards of acceptability and uniformity of
Entertainment Industry
procedures. In addition, the federal Government has a clear role to play in dealing with the importation of recorded material by virtue of its jurisdiction over customs.
Possibly the most significant federal interest in this matter is to ensure that if a system of review, classification and labelling of recorded material is necessary, it applies in one way or another throughout Canada and in accordance with the Charter. Although the direct participation of the federal Government in the administration of such a system may not be practicable, it is possible for Ottawa to establish a structure whereby the provinces eventually become obligated to act in this area subject to minimum standards.
It is with these thoughts in mind that I bring this matter before the House and ask that the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs be empowered to study the question of consumer standards for rating and labelling in the entertainment industry, particularly with respect to videos, records, cassette tapes and compact discs, and that in undertaking this study the committee focus on the question of sexually explicit lyrics and the negative moral effect this may be having on the youth of Canada.
